passages.title: Divorcing at the proper time and trusting Allah
passages.tafsir:
Sūrah aṭ-Ṭalāq opens by placing the most bitter moment in a marriage — the decision to end it — inside sacred law. Ayah 1 sets down when a divorce may be pronounced and where the woman stays afterwards; ayah 2 tells the husband what to do as her waiting period runs out; ayah 3 promises that whoever fears Allah through this ordeal will be given a way out and provision from a direction he never watched.

## Permitted, but hated

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes that in commercial matters the Qur'an sets down basic principles and rarely touches the bye-laws; in marriage and divorce it lays down the detailed laws, revealed directly by Allah. Islam has not treated marriage as a civil contract only, but has endowed it with the status of a kind of worship: a system of mutual rights and obligations, essential to family life and to bringing up children with upright conduct.

Divorce is permitted but hated. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān transmits from ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿUmar that of all permissible acts, divorce is the most detested one in the sight of Allah — so it should be used only as a last resort. It cites, from ʿAlī, the words of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "Marry; do not divorce, because divorce causes the Throne of the All-Merciful to shudder." And from Muʿādh ibn Jabal (via Qurṭubī), that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said Allah has created nothing on the face of the earth dearer to Him than the emancipation of slaves, and nothing more hateful to Him than divorce. If a marriage must end, it must end in a fair and dignified manner, never as a means of satisfying anger and revenge.

## "O Prophet" — one man addressed, a whole ummah instructed

The sūrah opens *yā ayyuhā an-Nabī*, "O Prophet," then switches to the plural: *idhā ṭallaqtum an-nisāʾ*, "when you (plural) divorce women." Ibn Kathīr says the Prophet ﷺ was addressed first to honour him, even though his ummah is also being addressed. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the grammar: Arabic has an *honorific* plural, in which a plural form is used of one person to express respect — so the plural verb honours the Prophet ﷺ while indicating that the injunction applies to the whole body of believers.

## Rule one: divorce her *for* her waiting period

*Fa-ṭalliqūhunna li-ʿiddatihinna* — "divorce them at (or for) their ʿiddah." *ʿIddah* means "to count"; in Sharīʿah it is the waiting period prescribed for a woman before she may marry another man. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lays out the categories: where the marriage ends by the husband's death, four months and ten days; where it ends by divorce and the woman is not pregnant, three menstrual periods according to Imām Abū Ḥanīfah, or three *ṭuhrs* (periods of purity after menses) according to Imām ash-Shāfiʿī — a difference hinging on how each reads *qurūʾ* in 2:228. So the command means: pronounce the divorce during *ṭuhr*, at a moment from which her ʿiddah can begin at once.

**The incident behind the ruling.** Al-Bukhārī recorded that ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿUmar divorced his wife during the lifetime of Allah's Messenger ﷺ while she was menstruating. ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb mentioned it to Allah's Messenger ﷺ, who became angry and said: "Order him to take her back and keep her until she is clean from her menses, and then to wait until she gets her next period and becomes clean again. Then, if he wishes to divorce her, he can divorce her when she is clean from her menses, before he has sexual intercourse with her. This is the ʿIddah which Allah the Exalted and Most Honored has fixed."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws four points: it is forbidden to divorce a woman while she is menstruating; if a man does so, he must retract the divorce, provided it is revocable, as it was in Ibn ʿUmar's case; if he divorces during the clean period he must not have had conjugal relations with her in it; and this is precisely the interpretation of *fa-ṭalliqūhunna li-ʿiddatihinna*.

**Why the timing matters.** Ibn Kathīr reports, through ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah from Ibn ʿAbbās: he does not divorce her while she is menstruating, nor during a purity in which he has had intercourse; rather he leaves her until her menses come and end, and then divorces her once. If she is divorced during her monthly course, that course is not counted; on the Ḥanafī view the following clean period is not counted either, so her ʿiddah only begins with her *next* menses. And divorcing after intercourse in a clean period risks divorcing a woman who may have conceived without either of them knowing.

**Two kinds of divorce.** In Ibn Kathīr's classification, the divorce conforming to the Sunnah is where the husband pronounces *one* divorce while she is not having her menses and without having had intercourse with her after the menses ended — or when it is clear that she is pregnant. The innovated divorce is one pronounced while she is menstruating, or after intercourse in a clean period while he does not know whether she has conceived. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that for the minor and the post-menopausal woman the ʿiddah is reckoned in months, and that the wife must not be unduly harmed by having her waiting period prolonged.

## Count, keep her home, and the one exception

*Wa aḥṣū al-ʿiddah* — "and count the ʿiddah." Ibn Kathīr: know its beginning and end, so that the ʿiddah does not become prolonged for the woman and leave her unable to marry again. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that the responsibility of keeping careful count is imposed on both men and women. Then *wa-ttaqū Allāha rabbakum*, "and have taqwā of Allah, your Lord" — Ibn Kathīr: in this matter.

*Lā tukhrijūhunna min buyūtihinna wa lā yakhrujna* — "do not expel them from their houses, nor should they leave." Ibn Kathīr explains that for the duration of the ʿiddah she has the right to housing from her husband; he may not force her out, nor is she allowed to leave, because she is still tied to the marriage contract. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws attention to the phrase "*their* houses": divorced women have a rightful claim in the home of their former husbands, and letting them reside there is no favour but one of the basic rights of a wife, continuing to the completion of the waiting period. Nor may she leave on her own, even if the husband permits it, because on the Ḥanafī view spending the ʿiddah in the house is not only the husband's right but a Divine right that Allah has imposed upon her.

The exception is *illā an yaʾtīna bi-fāḥishatin mubayyinah* — "unless they come up with a clearly shameless act." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records three views:

1. That leaving the husband's home on her own is itself the outright indecency — so the "exception" is not a real exception but an intensifier of the prohibition. This is ascribed to ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿUmar, as-Suddī, Ibn as-Sāʾib, an-Nakhaʿī and others, and Imām Abū Ḥanīfah has also preferred it (Rūḥ ul-Maʿānī).
2. That it refers to adultery: if she commits it and is proven guilty, she is taken out of the home for the prescribed punishment. This is attributed to Qatādah, al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, ash-Shaʿbī, Zayd ibn Aslam, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk, ʿIkrimah and others, and Imām Abū Yūsuf has preferred it. Ibn Kathīr likewise reports the adultery reading from ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿAbbās, Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib, ash-Shaʿbī, al-Ḥasan, Ibn Sīrīn, Mujāhid, ʿIkrimah, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk, Zayd ibn Aslam, as-Suddī and others.
3. That it refers to abusive language or quarrelling, so that a woman obscene in words and actions may be evicted from the home of her waiting period. This is ascribed to Ibn ʿAbbās on several chains, and confirmed by the reading of ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd and Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, *illā an yafḥushna*, whose apparent meaning is "indecent speech" (Rūḥ).

## "Those are the limits of Allah"

Ibn Kathīr: these are from His legislation and prohibitions; whoever violates them and implements anything else besides them *has wronged himself*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān unpacks the self-harm two ways. The religious loss is that he has sinned and will suffer for it in the Hereafter — he has not damaged Allah's law, only himself. The worldly loss is concrete: a man who divorces in violation of the rules will most probably end up with three pronouncements, after which it cannot be revoked; such a person regrets bitterly and suffers tremendous hardship in this world, especially if he has children. And many divorce their wives specifically intending to harm them; such cruel husbands are liable to a double punishment — for breaking Allah's sacred limits, and for the cruelty exercised.

**"You never know — perhaps Allah will bring about something new."** Ibn Kathīr explains *lā tadrī laʿalla Allāha yuḥdithu baʿda dhālika amran* as the wisdom of keeping her in the house: she remains during the ʿiddah so that the husband might regret his action, and Allah may decide that his heart turns again to the marriage continuing. Ibn Kathīr reports, through az-Zuhrī from ʿUbaydullāh ibn ʿAbdullāh, that Fāṭimah bint Qays glossed the "new thing" as *taking her back*, and that similar was said by ash-Shaʿbī, ʿAṭāʾ, Qatādah, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk, Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān and ath-Thawrī. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds the human texture: the husband may recall the comforts he enjoyed in his wife's company and the services she rendered in caring for the home and the children, and remorse does its work — but that door is only open if a *revocable* divorce was pronounced.

## Ayah 2: the decision at the edge of the waiting period

*Fa-idhā balaghna ajalahunna fa-amsikūhunna bi-maʿrūfin aw fāriqūhunna bi-maʿrūf.* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that *ajal* means the term of the ʿiddah, and "reaching the term" means *nearing its end*, not passing it. The timing is deliberate: by then the fit of anger should have dissipated, and the decision can be made with a cool and calm head.

The governing word is *maʿrūf*, "a recognised way" — the approved procedure of the Sharīʿah. Ibn Kathīr: if he reconciles, let it be while being kind to her in their companionship; if he divorces, let it be on good terms, without abusing, cursing or admonishing her. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes it practical. If the decision is to retain her, she should not be hurt afterwards in word or deed, nor should the reconciliation be held over her as a favour. If the decision is to release her, the ʿiddah is allowed to expire and she is released courteously.

**Keep the door open.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān derives a further rule: if a husband is forced into divorcing, it is the Divine will that he keep the option of revocation open. The approved method is to pronounce the divorce only *once*, in express and clear words, with no phrase of anger denoting absolute termination of the marriage tie. When such a phrase is used, or the words uttered with the intention of finality, the divorce takes effect at once and he loses the right of revocation; this is *ṭalāq bāʾin*. Worse still is pronouncing three divorces, after which he loses even the possibility of a fresh marriage contract by mutual agreement, as 2:230 states.

Imām an-Nasāʾī reports, on the authority of Maḥmūd ibn Labīd, in an authentic tradition, that the Prophet ﷺ was informed of a man who had pronounced three divorces on his wife on the spur of the moment, and he ﷺ became angry — so pronouncing three divorces simultaneously is, by consensus of the ummah, prohibited. Yet if a person does it anyway, all three take effect and a future marriage between them is not possible: the four major schools argue that a thing being unlawful does not mean its legal consequences do not follow.

**Witnesses.** *Wa ashhidū dhawāy ʿadlin minkum* — "and make two just men from among you witnesses." Ibn Kathīr says this refers to taking her back, if that is the decision. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports that according to most jurists this is *mustaḥabb* rather than mandatory, so revocation is not contingent upon it; its wisdom is to resolve disputes that may arise later — she may deny that he took her back, or he may falsely claim he did. *Aqīmū ash-shahādata lillāh*, "keep your testimony upright for the sake of Allah," addresses Muslims in general: if called to testify, be unbiased.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains why the Hereafter is invoked at the end of the ayah — the mutual rights and obligations of husband and wife cannot be fulfilled without consciousness of Allah and the thought of the Hereafter. Because of the delicate nature of the relationship, it is not possible to secure evidence for every shortcoming on either side, nor for any judicial system to estimate them. No police network can measure who fell short in a marriage; only taqwā can — hence the sūrah's rhythm, a ruling, then *and fear Allah, your Lord*. The very sermon recited at a marriage, it notes, is built of three verses of the Qur'an, each beginning and ending on taqwā.

## Ayah 3: the way out, and provision you did not see coming

*Wa man yattaqi Allāha yajʿal lahu makhrajan wa yarzuqhu min ḥaythu lā yaḥtasib.* Ibn Kathīr: whoever has taqwā of Allah in what He has commanded and avoids what He has forbidden, Allah will make a way out for him from every difficulty and will provide for him from resources he never anticipated. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that *taqwā* literally means "to guard" or "to refrain," and when related to Allah, "to avoid disobedience of Allah." Two benefits are promised: a way out — the "what from?" left general, covering all the difficulties of this world and the terrors of the next — and *rizq*, anything one needs, worldly or of the Hereafter, from where one does not expect it (Rūḥ).

Ibn Abī Ḥātim recorded that ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd said that the most comprehensive ayah in the Qur'an is 16:90, and *the greatest ayah in the Qur'an that contains relief* is this one. ʿIkrimah kept it tethered to the context: "Whoever divorces as Allah commanded him, then Allah will make a way out for him" — and similar was reported from Ibn ʿAbbās and aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk. Qatādah widened it: a way out from every doubt, and from the horrors at the time of death. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that some commentators read it of the divorcing husband and the divorced wife: Allah will deliver from the horrors of the separation, giving the man a compatible wife and the woman a compatible husband — though the primary meaning comprehends every kind of adversity (Rūḥ ul-Maʿānī).

**Its occasion of revelation.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports from ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAbbās that ʿAwf ibn Mālik al-Ashjaʿī came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and said the enemy had kidnapped his son Sālim and that the boy's mother was very anxious. The Prophet ﷺ ordered him and his wife to recite abundantly *lā ḥawla wa lā quwwata illā billāh* — "there is neither strength nor power but with Allah." They complied, and one day the enemy became unmindful, and the boy escaped and drove home a herd of their animals. On that occasion this verse was revealed. All these narratives are cited in Rūḥ ul-Maʿānī from Ibn Mardūyah, through the chain of al-Kalbī, from Ibn ʿAbbās. Though tied to a divorcing situation here, the verse has general application to all circumstances.

**Trust, and what it is not.** *Wa man yatawakkal ʿalā Allāhi fa-huwa ḥasbuh* — "and whosoever puts his trust in Allah, then He will suffice him." Ibn Kathīr places under this the ḥadīth Imām Aḥmad recorded from Ibn ʿAbbās, who rode the Prophet's camel sitting behind him ﷺ, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to him: "O boy! I will teach you words [so learn them]. Be mindful of Allah and He will protect you, be mindful of Allah and He will be on your side. If you ask, ask Allah, and if you seek help, seek it from Allah. Know that if the Ummah gather their strength to bring you benefit, they will never bring you benefit, except that which Allah has decreed for you. Know that if they gather their strength to harm you, they will never harm you, except with that which Allah has decreed against you. The pens have been raised and the pages are dry." At-Tirmidhī collected this ḥadīth and said: "Ḥasan Ṣaḥīḥ."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds what Tirmidhī and Ibn Mājah record from ʿUmar, that Allah's Messenger ﷺ said: "If you trust in Allah as He ought to be trusted, He will provide for you in the same way as He provides for the birds. They leave their nests while hungry in the mornings, but come back in the evenings with their bellies full."

The crucial qualification: *tawakkul* does not mean forsaking the causes and means Allah has created for us. Use the means at one's disposal — but instead of relying solely on them, put one's trust in Allah, knowing that no task is accomplished unless Allah wills it. The birds still leave the nest.

**Allah reaches His purpose.** *Inna Allāha bālighu amrih* — Ibn Kathīr: Allah will execute His decisions and judgement in whatever way He wills and chooses. *Qad jaʿala Allāhu li-kulli shayʾin qadran* — "Indeed Allah has set a measure for all things," which Ibn Kathīr pairs with "everything with Him is in due proportion" (13:8).

## Living it

This passage is remarkably gentle toward people at their worst. It slows the angry man down — wait for the right time, pronounce it once, keep it revocable — and refuses to let him throw her out of a house the Qur'an calls *hers*. And when the marriage still ends, it hands both of them the greatest ayah of relief in the Book: fear Allah, trust Allah, use the means — and expect the way out from a direction you were not watching.

passages.title: The remaining waiting periods, and the reward of the mindful
passages.tafsir:
These two ayat finish the picture of the waiting period (**ʿiddah**) after divorce. Sūrat al-Baqarah had already given the general rule — three menstrual cycles — but that rule assumed a woman who menstruates. Ayah 4 gathers up the women that rule did not cover: the one whose cycles have ended, the one whose cycles have not yet begun, and the one who is pregnant. Ayah 5 then stamps the whole body of these laws with divine authority — "That is the command of Allah, which He has sent down to you" — and closes, as ayah 4 did, on the same promise: whoever is mindful of Allah will find his affairs made easy, his sins wiped away, his reward enlarged. Law and reward are braided together here, and that braid is what holds the passage as one unit.

## The question that brought the answer down

Ibn Kathīr preserves something remarkable about this ayah: it came down as an answer to people who had read the earlier verse and noticed a gap.

Ubayy ibn Kaʿb said: "O Allah's Messenger! Some women were not mentioned in the Qur'an — the young, the old and the pregnant." And Allah sent down this ayah.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim records a simpler narration than this one, also from Ubayy ibn Kaʿb: when the ayah of Sūrat al-Baqarah was revealed prescribing the ʿiddah of divorce, some people in Madīnah said, "There are still some women whose ʿiddah has not been mentioned in the Qur'an. There are the young, the old whose menstruation is discontinued, and the pregnant." Later on, this ayah was revealed.

Notice how Allah answered — not with a rebuke for asking, but with a verse. The gap they felt was real, and the Qur'an closed it in the exact order they had raised it: the old, the young, the pregnant.

## The three categories in ayah 4

**Those who have despaired of menstruation.** The Arabic is *wa'llā'ī ya'isna mina'l-maḥīḍ* — rendered in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān as "those women from among you who have despaired of [further] menstruation." Ibn Kathīr defines her as the one whose menstruation has stopped due to her older age. Her ʿiddah is three months in place of the three monthly cycles prescribed for those who menstruate in Sūrat al-Baqarah [see 2:228].

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān widens the category slightly: women who have stopped menstruating for good on account of advanced age, *or due to some disease*, take the same three months. The operative fact is that the ordinary measure — the cycle — is no longer available, so Allah substitutes a calendar for it.

**Those who have not menstruated.** *Wa'llā'ī lam yaḥiḍn* — the young who have not reached the years of menstruation. Ibn Kathīr: their ʿiddah is three months, like those in menopause. The same substitution, from the other end of life. One woman's cycles have ended, the other's have not begun; both are given the same three-month measure.

**Those who are pregnant.** *Wa ulātu'l-aḥmāl ajaluhunna an yaḍaʿna ḥamlahunn* — "those who are pregnant: their ʿiddah is until they lay down their burden." The Qur'an does not say "three months" or "nine"; it fixes the end of the term to an event, not a number. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the consequence explicit: her ʿiddah continues until she gives birth to her child, *irrespective of the length of the period*. If the pregnancy is far along, her waiting may be short; if it is new, it may be many months. Her term is tied to a moment in her own body, not to a calendar.

## "If you are in doubt"

The phrase *ini'rtabtum*, "if you are in doubt," sits oddly in the middle of a legal ruling. Ibn Kathīr reports two opinions on it among the early scholars:

**First**, the saying of a group of the Salaf — Mujāhid, az-Zuhrī and Ibn Zayd: the doubt is about the *blood*. If such a woman sees blood and there is doubt whether it was menstrual blood or not, the ʿiddah is three months.

**Second**, reported from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr and preferred by Ibn Jarīr: the doubt is about the *ruling*. That is, if you do not know the ruling in this case, then know that their ʿiddah is three months. Ibn Kathīr calls this "the more obvious meaning," and cites in support of it the report of Ubayy ibn Kaʿb above — the report in which people were unsure which women the earlier verse had covered.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives a further explanation of the same words: the doubt or confusion is that which such women themselves may have, because the real ʿiddah is counted on the basis of menstruation, and their menstruation has ceased, so they are doubtful about how to count.

Where scholars explained a phrase differently like this, it is worth pausing over what does *not* change: on each of these explanations the ruling is the same — three months. The difference is about which uncertainty the verse is addressing, not about what a woman must do.

## The case of Subayʿah al-Aslamiyyah

Ibn Kathīr says that the pregnant woman's ʿiddah ends when she gives birth **whether in the case of divorce or the death of the husband**, according to the agreement of the majority of the scholars of the Salaf and later generations — and that this rests on this honourable ayah and on what is mentioned in the Prophetic Sunnah. That Sunnah is worth following closely, because you can watch a ruling being established.

**A man brings a hard case.** Abū Salamah reported — al-Bukhārī records it — that a man came to Ibn ʿAbbās, with Abū Hurayrah sitting beside him, and asked for a verdict about a lady who delivered a baby forty days after the death of her husband. Ibn ʿAbbās said her waiting lasts until the end of the longest among the two prescribed periods. Abū Salamah recited: *"For those who are pregnant, their prescribed period is until they deliver their burdens."* Abū Hurayrah said, "I agree with my cousin."

**The matter is referred to a witness.** Ibn ʿAbbās then sent his slave Kurayb to Umm Salamah to ask her. She replied that the husband of Subayʿah al-Aslamiyyah was killed while she was pregnant; she delivered a baby forty days after his death; she then received a marriage proposal, and Allah's Messenger ﷺ married her to somebody. Abū as-Sanābil was one of those who proposed to her. Al-Bukhārī collected this short form of the ḥadīth, and Ibn Kathīr notes that Muslim and other scholars of ḥadīth collected its longer form.

**Subayʿah's own account.** Muslim ibn al-Ḥajjāj records the longer version, obtained by written enquiry: ʿUbaydullāh ibn ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿUtbah related that his father wrote to ʿUmar ibn ʿAbdullāh ibn al-Arqam az-Zuhrī, asking him to go to Subayʿah bint al-Ḥārith al-Aslamiyyah herself and ask her about the matter, and about what Allah's Messenger ﷺ had said to her when she sought his verdict. ʿUmar wrote back with her testimony. She had been married to Saʿd ibn Khawlah, one of those who participated in the battle of Badr. He died during the Farewell Pilgrimage while she was pregnant. Soon after his death she gave birth. When she passed the postnatal term, she beautified herself for those who might propose to her. Abū as-Sanābil ibn Baʿkak came to her and said, "Why do I see you have beautified yourself? Do you wish to remarry? By Allah, you cannot marry unless four months and ten days have passed."

Then Subayʿah says: "When he said that, I dressed myself in the evening and went to Allah's Messenger ﷺ and asked him about his verdict. He gave me a religious verdict that I was allowed to marry after I had given birth to my child, saying I could marry if I wish."

Imām Aḥmad also records, from al-Miswar ibn Makhramah, that Subayʿah gave birth to a child a few days after the death of her husband, and when she finished the post-delivery term she was proposed to; she sought the permission of Allah's Messenger ﷺ for the marriage, and he permitted her, so she married. Ibn Kathīr notes that al-Bukhārī collected this narration, as did Muslim, Abū Dāwūd, an-Nasā'ī and Ibn Mājah, with a different chain of narration from the ḥadīth of Subayʿah.

Several things are worth carrying away from this. A confident man told a bereaved woman what the law was, swearing by Allah that she could not marry for four months and ten days — and the Messenger ﷺ ruled otherwise. She did not simply accept his word and she did not simply defy it: she went that same evening and asked. And when Ibn ʿAbbās and those sitting with him differed over the very same question, the way forward was again to ask the women who had been there — Umm Salamah, and then Subayʿah herself. What settled the matter was the plain word of ayah 4 and the verdict of the Prophet ﷺ upon it: *their term is that they lay down their burden.*

## The refrain: "whoever is mindful of Allah"

Twice in this short passage the legal ruling gives way to a promise about **taqwā** — the mindfulness of a person who keeps Allah before his eyes and guards himself from crossing His limits.

At the end of ayah 4: *wa man yattaqi'llāha yajʿal lahu min amrihi yusrā* — "whosoever has taqwā of Allah, He will make his matter easy for him." Ibn Kathīr explains: Allah will make his matters lenient for him and will soon bring forth relief and a quick way out. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that this ease is promised in this world *as well as in the next*.

That promise is placed exactly where a person needs it. These rulings arrive in the middle of a marriage coming apart — the point at which holding a limit costs something. Allah does not simply issue the limit and leave the person with the cost; He attaches a promise to it: hold to what I have commanded, and I will open your way.

## "That is the command of Allah" (ayah 5)

Ayah 5 opens by putting a seal on everything that has come: *dhālika amru'llāhi anzalahu ilaykum*. Ibn Kathīr: this is His commandment and His legislation that He sent down to you through His Messenger ﷺ. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads the same words as an emphasis on strict adherence to the laws of divorce and the waiting period just given.

The force of the word *anzalahu*, "He sent it down," is worth feeling. These are not community customs about family life, adjustable by preference. They came down. Ibn ʿAbbās's caution and Abū as-Sanābil's certainty both had to yield to what had come down and to what the Messenger ﷺ ruled on its basis.

Then, immediately, the promise a second time: *wa man yattaqi'llāha yukaffir ʿanhu sayyi'ātihi wa yuʿẓim lahu ajrā* — "whosoever has taqwā of Allah, He will expiate from him his sins, and will increase his reward." Ibn Kathīr's gloss is beautiful in its economy: Allah will prevent what he fears, and multiply his reward even for the little good he does. Both sides of a person's account are addressed — the debts are cancelled, and the small credits are enlarged.

A man counting out three months over a marriage that has ended, or a woman waiting until she gives birth before her life can move on, is being asked for real patience. So Allah does not merely command; He rewards.

## Five blessings of taqwā

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gathers the merits and blessings of taqwā mentioned in these verses into five things. Whoever has taqwā:

1. will be given a way out of difficulties and adversities;
2. will be provided with all his needs from resources he does not anticipate or expect;
3. will have his matters and tasks made easy by Allah;
4. will have his sins expiated;
5. will be granted an immense reward.

And it points to one more blessing of taqwā named elsewhere in the Qur'an: the person mindful of Allah finds it easier to distinguish between right and wrong — *"If you fear Allah, He will provide you with a criterion (furqān)"* [8:29].

Read that list back against the passage. Every one of those five is offered in the middle of a discussion about marriages that are ending — the very place where keeping the limit is hardest.

## Living it

- **The law fits the person's real condition.** Three cycles for the one who has cycles; three months for the one who does not; birth for the one who is pregnant. Where a measure cannot apply, Allah gives another.
- **Ask, don't assume.** The people of Madīnah raised the categories the earlier verse had not named, and Subayʿah asked rather than accept a confident stranger's ruling. Both times, asking produced clarity and ease.
- **When you are counting out a hard obligation, count on the promise attached to it.** Ayah 4 and ayah 5 both end the same way. Ease in your affair, sins wiped out, reward enlarged — that is what is on offer to the one who keeps Allah's limits in exactly the place where limits are hardest to keep.

passages.title: Housing, nursing wages, and spending by means
passages.tafsir:
These two ayat take the law of divorce down to the level of daily life: a roof, a meal, a baby's feed, and a monthly sum of money. Ayah 6 governs the waiting period itself — where she lives, how she must be treated, what she is owed while pregnant, and what happens when the child is born and needs nursing. Ayah 7 then answers the question every one of those duties raises: *how much?* The thread running through the passage is the phrase **"according to his means"** — obligations that are real and enforceable, yet calibrated to what a man actually has, and sealed with a promise from Allah that hardship is not the end of the story.

## Ayah 6: a roof, not a favour

**"Lodge them where you dwell, according to what you have."**

Ibn Kathir explains that Allah is ordering His believing servants that when one of them divorces his wife, he must provide her housing until her ʿiddah (waiting period) ends — and that *"where you dwell"* means **with you**, in the same residence.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that this is the positive face of an injunction already given earlier in the surah: divorced women must not be turned out of their homes. Ayah 6 states the same duty from the other side — not merely "do not expel her," but "house her."

**"min wujdikum" — according to what you have.** Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid and several others glossed this as *"your ability."* Qatadah put it with unforgettable practicality: *"If you can only afford to accommodate her in a corner of your house, then do so."* The obligation is never waived for poverty; it is scaled to it. A man with one room owes her that corner.

**A note on modesty inside the shared home.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws an important distinction. If the divorce is revocable (rajʿī) — meaning the marriage tie still stands and he may take her back — no hijab is required between them. But if it is irrevocable, whether of the lesser degree (*baʼin*) or by the pronouncement of three divorces, the marriage tie is broken and she must observe hijab before her former husband. The living arrangement therefore has to be organised so that she remains in the same residence *with full observance of the rules of hijab*. The Qur'an keeps her housed and keeps her honour intact at the same time.

## "And do not harm them in order to straiten them"

The next clause forbids weaponising that shared roof.

Ibn Kathir cites **Muqatil bin Hayyan**: it means *"do not annoy her to force her to pay her way out, nor expel her from your house."* That is, do not make life so unpleasant that she buys her freedom or walks out — surrendering money or rights just to escape the atmosphere.

Then a second, subtler form of cruelty. **Ath-Thawri narrated from Mansur, from Abu Ad-Duha**, on this same phrase: *"He divorces her, and when a few days remain, he takes her back."* The man does nothing openly abusive. He simply waits until her waiting period is nearly over, revokes the divorce, then divorces again — resetting the clock, holding her suspended indefinitely. The Qur'an names that manoeuvre as *ḍarar*, harm, even though every individual step in it is technically lawful.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sums up the whole prohibition: she must not be harassed by taunts, nor by the curtailing of the things she needs, so that she is compelled to leave the home. Both the tongue and the household budget can be used as instruments of pressure, and both are forbidden here.

## Maintenance while she is pregnant

**"And if they are pregnant, then spend on them until they lay down their burden."**

Ibn Kathir specifies that this clause is speaking about the **irrevocably** divorced woman: if she is pregnant, she is to be maintained until she delivers. He explains the reasoning — the revocably divorced woman already has the right to maintenance whether pregnant or not, so the verse is addressing the case that would otherwise be in doubt.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records that on the basis of this verse there is **complete consensus of the Ummah** that the pregnant divorcee's maintenance is obligatory on the husband. Likewise, all the jurists of the Ummah agree that a non-pregnant woman under a revocable divorce must be maintained until her ʿiddah expires.

**Where the scholars differed.** The disputed case is the woman irrevocably divorced (*baʼin*, or by three pronouncements), or one who has obtained separation through *khulʿ* (release from the marriage in return for compensation). According to Imam ash-Shafiʿi, Imam Ahmad and others, the husband does not owe her maintenance. According to **Imam Abu Hanifah**, he does. His argument, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān presents it, is drawn straight from this ayah: since she is entitled to *residence* during the ʿiddah by the text of ayah 6, she is entitled to *sustenance* on the same footing — both are necessities of life the husband is obligated to supply during that period.

The commentary adds the supporting report: when Sayyidna **ʿUmar** heard the account of Fatimah bint Qais, who held that her husband owed her no maintenance after the divorce, he said, *"We cannot abandon the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of the Prophet ﷺ on the basis of this narration."* [Muslim] "The Book of Allah" here apparently refers to this very ayah — ʿUmar understood it to include maintenance. "The Sunnah" refers to a tradition ʿUmar himself reported, transmitted by Tahawi, Darqutni and Tabarani, that women divorced by three pronouncements are also entitled to maintenance and lodging. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān refers the reader to *Tafsir Mazhari* for the details.

This is a genuine difference among the imams; the Qur'an's own words settle the housing and the pregnant woman's support beyond dispute, and the remaining case is where the schools part.

## The child is born: wages for nursing

**"Then if they suckle the children for you, give them their due payment."**

Ibn Kathir explains that once the pregnant woman gives birth, her ʿiddah has expired and the separation is complete — so at that point she *may* nurse the child or she may not. It is now her choice, not her duty. But he adds a crucial qualification: this freedom comes only **after she has given him the early milk** on which the infant's wellbeing depends. Beyond that, if she nurses, she has a right to be paid for it, and she may enter a contract with the father or his representative for whatever payment they agree upon.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the underlying legal logic beautifully. While the marriage is intact, nursing the child is the mother's own responsibility — as the Qur'an says elsewhere, *"And the mothers suckle their children"* (2:233). One cannot take a fee for performing what is already obligatory upon one; that would amount to *rishwah*, bribery, unlawful to give or to take. The ʿiddah period is like the marriage in this respect, because the husband is obliged to maintain her throughout it, so she cannot charge for nursing then either. But once she delivers, her ʿiddah is over and she is absolutely released from the marriage tie; he no longer owes her maintenance. From that moment, the ayah permits a payment to be given and taken for her service — and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that if she claims that fee, it is incumbent upon her former husband to pay it.

## "And consult one another with fairness"

**"waʼtamirū baynakum bi-maʿrūf."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that *iʼtimār* means to consult one another and to accept each other's suggestion. The instruction is aimed at the fee: the divorced wife should not demand more than the normal rate, and the former husband should not refuse to pay the normal rate. They are advised to settle it with mutual understanding and tolerance.

Ibn Kathir reads it more broadly: the affairs of the divorced couple should be managed justly, without causing harm to either one of them — exactly as Allah said in Surat al-Baqarah, *"No mother shall be treated unfairly on account of her child, nor father on account of his child"* (2:233). Note the symmetry in that verse: the child is not to become a lever against either parent. That principle is the moral engine of this whole passage.

## If they reach deadlock

**"But if you make difficulties for one another, then another woman may suckle for him."**

Ibn Kathir: if the couple cannot agree — she asks an unreasonable fee, or he refuses to pay it or offers an unreasonable amount — the father may engage another woman to nurse his child. But he adds the balancing clause: **if the mother agrees to accept the amount that was to be paid to the other woman, then she has more right to nurse her own child.**

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the human wisdom here. If they cannot agree on the fee, or the mother refuses to nurse even for a payment, **no court can compel her**. Normally a mother has the most compassion for her child; if she is nonetheless refusing, she probably has a genuine reason. If she has no genuine reason and refuses merely out of anger and displeasure, she is a sinner in the sight of Allah — but an Islamic court still cannot force her to nurse. Equally, if the husband, through abject poverty, cannot pay the fee, and a wet-nurse is willing to nurse without remuneration or for less than the mother demands, he cannot be forced to meet her demand. And if the fee the mother asks equals the wet-nurse's, **preference is given to the mother** — a point of consensus among all the Muslim jurists.

There is a further ruling from *Tafsir Mazhari*: if a wet-nurse is engaged, she must nurse the child **while the child remains in the custody of the mother**. It is not lawful to separate mother and baby, because custody (*ḥiḍānah*) is the mother's right as stated in the authentic Traditions, and it is not permissible to usurp that right from her.

Read the two provisions together and the balance is striking: the law will not force a mother's body, and it will not tear her child from her arms either.

## Ayah 7: "Let the man of means spend according to his means"

**"Let the rich man spend according to his means; and the man whose resources are restricted, let him spend from what Allah has given him."**

Ibn Kathir applies it directly: the wealthy father, or his representative, should spend on the child according to his means. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān applies it to the quantum of the divorcee's maintenance — the husband's financial position is what determines the amount. If he is wealthy, he spends in keeping with his affluence; if he is indigent, he spends in keeping with his limited resources, **even if the wife herself is wealthy**. This, the commentary notes, is the ruling of Imam Abu Hanifah; other schools of jurisprudence hold differing views [Tafsir Mazhari].

Two things are protected at once. The poor man is not crushed by a standard he cannot meet, and the rich man cannot hide behind a minimum. "According to his means" cuts in both directions.

**"Allah does not burden any soul beyond what He has given it."** Ibn Kathir places this alongside *"Allah does not burden a person beyond what he can bear"* (2:286). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls it an elaboration of the preceding statement: Allah does not demand from anyone more than he can afford. The practical conclusion follows — if the husband is indigent, it is incumbent upon him to provide for her according to his level of indigence **at that time**.

## "Allah will bring ease after hardship"

The ayah does not end with the poor man's limitation; it ends with a promise. Ibn Kathir calls it **a sure promise from Him** — and Allah's promises are true and He never breaks them — placing it beside *"Verily, along with every hardship is relief. Verily, along with every hardship is relief"* (94:5–6).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān turns the promise toward the wife: she is advised to be content, for the time being, with what her indigent husband is able to provide, and not to think that his present state will last for all times to come — because ease and difficulty are in the hands of Allah, and He can change indigence into affluence.

And it turns the promise toward the husband too. Citing *Ruh-ul-Maʿani*, the commentary notes that the verse bears an indication that **Allah will create a condition of ease for husbands who try to provide their wives the obligatory amount of sustenance to the best of their ability, and who are not in the habit of keeping their wives under straitened circumstances.** The ease is promised to the man who genuinely tries — not to the man who pleads poverty while squeezing her.

**A story of a woman who had taqwa.** Ibn Kathir closes with a narration recorded by **Imam Ahmad** from Abu Hurayrah. A man and his wife of an earlier generation were poor. He came back from a journey, hungry and fatigued, and asked her whether she had anything to eat. She said, "Yes — receive the good news of Allah's provisions." He pressed her; she said, "Wait a little longer," awaiting Allah's mercy. When the matter was prolonged and he insisted again, she said she would soon open the oven's cover and told him not to be hasty. When he was busy and refrained from insisting for a while, she said to herself, "I should look in my oven" — and she found it full of the meat of a lamb, and her mortar and pestle full of seed grains, crushing the seeds on its own. She took out what was in the mortar and pestle, after shaking it to remove everything from inside, and took out the meat she had found in the oven.

Abu Hurayrah then swore by the One in whose Hand is the life of Abu al-Qasim ﷺ that this matched what the Prophet ﷺ said: *"Had she taken out what was in her mortar and not emptied it fully by shaking it, it would have continued crushing the seeds until the Day of Resurrection."*

Her line — *"receive the good news of Allah's provisions"* — is the perfect commentary on the ayah's closing words. She held her tongue from complaint and held her heart on Allah, and the ease came.

## Living it

- **House her.** Even a corner, if that is all you have. The obligation is scaled to your means, never cancelled by them.
- **Do not use the shared roof as a weapon** — not through taunts, not through withholding what she needs, not through the trick of revoking the divorce at the last moment to restart her waiting.
- **Support the pregnant divorcee until she delivers.** The whole Ummah agrees on this.
- **Pay for nursing** once her ʿiddah has ended, at a fair rate — and if you are the mother, do not price your own child out of your arms.
- **Talk it through with maʿrūf** — mutual consultation, mutual give. Neither parent may be harmed through the child.
- **Spend to the limit of what Allah has actually given you**, and trust the closing promise: *sayajʿalu-llāhu baʿda ʿusrin yusrā* — Allah will bring, after hardship, ease.

passages.title: Towns that defied their Lord and tasted ruin
passages.tafsir:
These two ayat are a warning drawn from history. Allah points to the wreckage of earlier communities — town after town that heard the command of its Lord, refused it, and was called to account. Ayah 8 states what those towns did and what was done to them; ayah 9 states what came of it and what it added up to in the end. Together they form one movement: **rebellion → reckoning → the taste of ruin → loss.**

Ibn Kathir's treatment of these ayat runs under the heading "Punishment for defying Allah's Commandments," and he sets their purpose plainly: Allah "threatens those who defy His commands, deny His Messengers and contradict His legislation, by informing them of the end that earlier nations met who did the same." So the ayat are not history recounted for its own sake. On Ibn Kathir's reading they are aimed at a living listener — a warning, delivered by showing him what happened to people who took the position he may be tempted to take.

## "And many a town…"

The passage opens: **وَكَأَيِّن مِّن قَرْيَةٍ** — rendered in the translation before us as *And many a town*. Not one town. Ibn Kathir speaks in the plural throughout — "earlier nations," "the disbelieving nations" — so what is being held up is a pattern, repeated across communities, not a single episode.

Notice too that the ayah's subject is a **قَرْيَة**, a town — a community rather than an individual — and yet the grammar keeps sliding between the town and the people in it. The ayah says the town "revolted" and the town "tasted," while Ibn Kathir's explanation shifts to the plural: *they* rebelled, *they* tasted. The town is its people. A community is named, but it is human beings who feel it.

## عَتَتْ — what the rebellion was

The verb rendered *revolted* carries the whole indictment, and Ibn Kathir unpacks it in three strokes: they **rebelled**, they **rejected**, and they **arrogantly refused to obey Allah** — "and they would not follow His Messengers."

That third stroke is the one to sit with. What is described here is not the failure of a weak person who wants to obey and falls short. Ibn Kathir's words are *arrogantly refused* — refusal with the chin raised, a settled unwillingness to be told what to do. And the ayah specifies whose command was refused: **عَنْ أَمْرِ رَبِّهَا** — the command of *its Lord*. The One they revolted against is the very One named as their Lord.

## "…and His Messengers"

The command defied is that of "its Lord **and His Messengers**." The two are joined in the ayah, and Ibn Kathir's gloss keeps them welded together in a single sentence: they "arrogantly refused to obey Allah and they would not follow His Messengers." His opening statement pairs them the same way — those who "defy His commands, **deny His Messengers** and contradict His legislation."

This is worth pausing over, because it is exactly the move people still make: a claimed loyalty to Allah alongside a practical refusal of the concrete instructions He actually sent. On the reading of this ayah, that is not two separate matters. It is one posture.

## فَحَاسَبْنَاهَا حِسَابًا شَدِيدًا — the severe account

*And We called it to a severe account, and We shall punish it with a horrible torment.* Ibn Kathir's comment on that punishment is brief and heavy: **"horrendous and terrifying."**

**When does this happen?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pauses here on a real difficulty in the wording: the ayah uses the **past tense** — *We called them to account, We punished them* — for what one would expect to lie in the future. It offers three ways the ayah has been read, and it is worth having all three, because the scholars genuinely differed:

1. **Both belong to the Hereafter.** The severe account and the evil punishment refer to what will happen in the Hereafter; the past tense is used "to indicate the occurrence of these events is as certain as if it has already been materialised." Maʿārif attributes this to *Rūḥ*.
2. **"Account" here is not interrogation but the fixing of the sentence.** On this possibility, *ḥisāb* means "the determination of punishment" — in which case, Maʿārif notes, it may refer to punishment faced by the disbelievers "right here in this world."
3. **The account belongs to the Hereafter, but it is already being written.** The severe account will take place in the Hereafter, "it has already been recorded and is being recorded on daily basis in the ledger of deeds," and so it can be spoken of in the past tense already. On this reading, Maʿārif says, the "punishment" refers to past nations destroyed by divine punishment in this world "because they defied Allah's and His Messengers' commandments" — and it is only the later statement **أَعَدَّ اللَّهُ لَهُمْ عَذَابًا شَدِيدًا**, *Allah has prepared for them a severe punishment*, that refers to the punishment of the Hereafter.

The ayah stands on any of these three. But the third has a particular bite for a living reader: on that reading the file is open now, added to daily. Nothing waits until the Day to be entered; the Day is when it is read out.

## فَذَاقَتْ وَبَالَ أَمْرِهَا — the taste

Ayah 9 does not say they *received* the consequence. It says they **tasted** it: *So it tasted the evil result of its affair*. Ibn Kathir renders it in the plural and makes it concrete — "they tasted the evil consequences of defiance."

And note whose affair it was: **أَمْرِهَا**, *its* affair — their own conduct, coming back to them. What they taste is not something foreign; it is the result of what they themselves did.

Then Ibn Kathir adds the detail that makes the ayah ache. They tasted the evil consequences of defiance "**and they regretted their actions when regret does not avail**." Regret arrives — but it arrives after the door has shut. The tragedy of these towns, on Ibn Kathir's telling, is not that they never came to see it. It is that the seeing came at a point where it no longer helped.

## وَكَانَ عَاقِبَةُ أَمْرِهَا خُسْرًا — loss

The ayah closes by naming the bottom line: *and the consequence of its affair was loss*. **خُسْرًا** — loss. That is the whole verdict, stated without adornment: not a mixed result, not a gain with regrettable costs. Loss.

And Ibn Kathir does not let the reader think the account closes with the ruins. His comment runs on into the statement that immediately follows — *And Allah has prepared for them a severe torment* — and he explains it as meaning "**in the Hereafter, added to** the torment that was sent down on them in this life." The destruction of a defiant town was not the punishment paid in full. On this reading it was an instalment, with more prepared beyond it.

## Living it

**Take the ruins as a warning aimed at you.** Ibn Kathir states the purpose of the passage outright: Allah threatens those who defy His commands by informing them of the end earlier nations met. The ayat are told to be applied — the reader is the one being addressed by the ruins, not merely informed about them.

**Watch for arrogant refusal in its quiet forms.** Ibn Kathir's three words are *rebelled, rejected, arrogantly refused* — and among those he names as threatened here are people who "contradict His legislation." Contradicting the legislation rarely announces itself; it shows up as treating a clear command as negotiable, an inconvenient ruling quietly set aside.

**Do not split Allah from His Messengers.** The ayah fuses the command of the Lord with the command of His Messengers, and Ibn Kathir's gloss keeps them fused. Reverence for Allah that stops short of following what He actually sent is the very posture named here.

**Do not bank on future regret.** The one thing these towns eventually acquired was remorse — "when regret does not avail." Remorse is not the problem; its timing is. The mercy of a passage like this is that it hands you the ending before you have finished writing the story.

**Run the account to its consequence, not its middle.** The verdict of ayah 9 is reached at the end: *the consequence of its affair was loss*. And on Maʿārif's third reading, that account is being written into the ledger of deeds daily — which means today's entry is one you are still choosing.

passages.title: The Reminder sent down to those of understanding
passages.tafsir:
Surah At-Talaq ends with a warning, a gift, and a view of the whole universe. Ayat 10–12 take the reader from the ruin of nations that defied their Lord, to the Reminder and the Messenger ﷺ Allah has sent to this community, to the seven heavens and their like of earth through which His command descends. What holds them together is a single argument: *the One who legislates is the One who owns and governs everything* — so take His law seriously.

## The warning that sets it up (ayah 10a)

Ayah 10 opens mid-thought. The verses just before it describe towns that "revolted against the command of its Lord and His Messengers," were "called to a severe account," and "tasted the evil result of its affair." Ibn Kathir explains that Allah is here threatening "those who defy His commands, deny His Messengers and contradict His legislation, by informing them of the end that earlier nations met who did the same." Those nations "rebelled, rejected and arrogantly refused to obey Allah and they would not follow His Messengers," and the punishment described was "horrendous and terrifying." When they finally tasted the consequences, "they regretted their actions when regret does not avail" — regret arrives, but too late to be of any use.

Then comes ayah 10: **"Allah has prepared for them a severe torment."** Ibn Kathir is precise about what this adds. The destruction those nations met was in this world; this severe torment is "in the Hereafter, added to the torment that was sent down on them in this life." The account is not closed by a ruined city. There is a second reckoning waiting.

## "So have Taqwa of Allah, O men of understanding" (ayah 10b)

Only now does the address swing round to us. The Arabic is **ulū al-albāb**, rendered by Ibn Kathir as "men of understanding" and again as "people of comprehension." He gives the sense of the command like this: *"O you who have sound understanding, do not be like them because if you do, you will suffer what they suffered, O people of comprehension."*

That is the whole logic of the phrase. History has just been laid out as evidence. To have a functioning mind is simply to look at what happened to those who defied Allah and decline to walk the same road. **Taqwā** — the word translated here as fearing Allah, or as Ibn Kathir renders it, "have Taqwa of Allah" — is presented not as a mood but as the conclusion an intelligent person draws once he has read the record honestly.

The address then narrows further: **"those who believe."** Ibn Kathir glosses this as believing "in Allah and His Messengers." So the ayah is speaking to people who already have faith. The warning is not only for the rejecter; the believer too is being told, in effect, *you have seen what happened — now let that knowledge weigh on how you treat Allah's commands.*

## The Reminder and the Messenger (ayat 10c–11)

**"Allah has indeed sent down to you a Reminder."** Ibn Kathir identifies the *Dhikr* here plainly: "this Qur'an." He supports it with Allah's own words elsewhere — *"Verily, We, it is We Who have sent down the Dhikr and surely, We will preserve it"* (15:9) — where *Dhikr* likewise names the revealed Book, along with Allah's pledge to guard it.

Then ayah 11 begins with a single word standing on its own: **rasūlan**, "a messenger." The grammar of this has occupied the commentators, and it is worth seeing why.

**The straightforward reading.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that the verb *arsala* ("sent") is to be understood before the object *rasūlan*, so the two ayat read: "Allah has sent down to you a Reminder, (the Qur'an, and He has also sent to you) a messenger." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls this "the simplest way in which these verses can be interpreted." Two gifts, one after the other — the Book, and the man who brings it.

**The other reading.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records that other commentators preferred other interpretations. "For instance some say that the word *dhikr* ('Reminder') refers to the Holy Prophet ﷺ himself, and the word 'messenger' is an explanatory complement to the word 'dhikr', because abundance of his remembering Allah made him a personified Remembrance of Allah." On that reading, the Prophet ﷺ is called the Reminder because remembrance of Allah so filled his life.

A footnote signed *Muhammad Taqi Usmani* adds a clarification: that explanation rests on taking *dhikr* here to mean "Allah's remembrance." But *dhikr* also means "reminder," and taken in that sense the identification is easier still — "messenger" can be read as an explanatory complement to "Reminder" because the Holy Prophet ﷺ *is* a Reminder to the entire mankind. The translation given in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān follows this second sense.

Both readings converge on the same lived reality: you do not receive this religion as a text alone. It reaches you through a person.

**What the Messenger does.** Ibn Kathir reports a related discussion. Some said the Messenger is the subject of what is sent as a reminder, because he is the one who conveys the *Dhikr*. Ibn Jarir said that what is correct is that **the Messenger explains the Dhikr** — and Ibn Kathir notes this is why the ayah continues: *"A Messenger, who recites to you the Ayat of Allah containing clear explanations."*

Those clear explanations, Ibn Kathir glosses, means "plain and apparent." The revelation does not arrive as a riddle. It arrives clarified — and it arrives through a reciter who explains it. This is a quiet but important point for anyone who imagines the Qur'an was meant to be approached without the Messenger ﷺ: the ayah itself pairs them.

## Out of the darkness into the light (ayah 11)

The purpose clause is one of the most beautiful in the Qur'an: **"that He may take out those who believe and do righteous good deeds, from the darkness to the light."**

Ibn Kathir sets it beside two sister ayat:

- *"A Book which We have revealed unto you in order that you might lead mankind out of darkness"* (14:1)
- *"Allah is the Guardian of those who believe. He brings them out from darkness into light"* (2:257)

And he gives the meaning: **out of the darkness of disbelief and ignorance into the light of faith and knowledge.**

Note who is brought out: "those who believe **and do righteous good deeds**." Belief and action are named together, as they will be again at the end of the ayah. The exit from darkness is not achieved by assent alone.

**Why revelation is called light — and called Rūḥ.** Ibn Kathir observes that Allah called the revelation He sent down *light* "on account of the guidance that it brings," and called it *Rūḥ* (spirit), "in that, it brings life to the hearts." He cites: *"And thus We have sent to you Ruh of Our command. You knew not what is the book, nor what is faith? But We have made it a light wherewith We guide whosoever of Our servants We will. And verily, you are indeed guiding to the straight path"* (42:52).

Two images, two different needs. Light is what a person needs who cannot see. Life is what a person needs who is not alive. The revelation is described as both — and this same ayah underlines that even the Prophet ﷺ "knew not what is the book, nor what is faith" until Allah gave it to him.

**The outcome.** The ayah ends: *"And whosoever believes in Allah and performs righteous good deeds, He will admit him into Gardens under which rivers flow, to dwell therein forever. Allah has indeed granted for him an excellent provision."* Ibn Kathir notes that this promise "was explained several times before," and so he does not repeat it here. Set it against the opening of ayah 10 — "Allah has prepared for them a severe torment." A severe torment prepared, an excellent provision granted; the whole passage stands between the two, and the conditions named for the second are the same two throughout: believe, and act rightly.

## Seven heavens, and the like of them from earth (ayah 12)

The surah's final ayah pulls back to the scale of creation: **"It is Allah Who has created seven heavens and of the earth the like thereof. His command descends between them, that you may know that Allah has power over all things, and that Allah surrounds all things with (His) knowledge."**

Ibn Kathir explains *why* the surah closes this way: "Allah the Exalted asserts His perfect power and infinite greatness, **so that the great religion that He has legislated is honored and implemented**." The cosmology is not a change of subject. It is the enforcement clause. The One who legislates is the One who made the seven heavens and their like of earth, who has power over all things and surrounds all things with His knowledge.

**The seven heavens.** Ibn Kathir cites what Prophet Nuh said to his people, *"See you not how Allah has created the seven heavens one above another?"* (71:15), and *"The seven heavens and the earth and all that is therein, glorify Him"* (17:44).

**The seven earths.** On *"and of the earth the like thereof,"* Ibn Kathir states the meaning directly: it means He created seven earths. He supports it from the Sunnah. In the Two Sahihs there is a hadith that states: *"Whoever usurps the land of somebody unjustly, even if it was a mere hand span, then his neck will be encircled with it down to the seven earths."* And in Sahih Al-Bukhari the wording is: *"…he will sink down to the seven earths."*

Ibn Kathir mentions that he gathered the various narrations of this hadith at the beginning of his book *Al-Bidayah wan-Nihayah*, when he narrated the story of the creation of the earth. He also rejects a competing reading: those who explained this hadith to mean the seven continents "have brought an implausible explanation that contradicts the letter of the Qur'an and the Hadith without having proof."

There is a moral edge here that is easy to miss. The scale of Allah's creation is established, in Ibn Kathir's presentation, by way of a hadith about **land theft** — a stolen hand span of soil. The immensity of what Allah has made is invoked in the very breath that warns against a small, mean injustice.

## "Leave unexplained what Allah has left unexplained"

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān takes up the obvious question: this ayah indicates that there are seven earths as there are seven heavens — but where are they, and in what shape or form? Are they layers one above the other, or is each earth separate? If they are layers, is there distance between them as there is between two heavens? Are there separate creatures living on each earth, as separate types of angels reside in every heaven? Is there air, wind and atmosphere on each? Or are the layers joined and compact?

The answer given is disciplined, and worth learning as a method:

- **The Qur'an is silent on all of it.** There are traditions reported on these questions, but the leading authorities of hadith disagree about their authenticity; some scholars authenticated them, others graded them as "fabricated."
- **Rationally, all findings are possible** — nothing forces one answer.
- **Nothing depends on it.** None of our religious or worldly needs are dependent on resolving these issues, nor will we be questioned about them in the grave or at the Resurrection.
- **The safest position** is simply to believe that there are seven earths as there are seven skies, created by Allah with His Supreme Creative Power. The Qur'an has mentioned this much only; if the Qur'an did not find it necessary to give a detailed account of it, there is no need for us to research it.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports that this was the attitude of the pious predecessors, who formulated the policy: **"Leave unexplained what Allah has left unexplained"** — as long as it contains no injunction for us to follow and concerns no religious or worldly need of ours.

This is a genuinely freeing discipline. Curiosity about the unseen can quietly become a substitute for obedience in the seen. The ayah did not mention the seven earths so that we would map them; it mentioned them, as Ibn Kathir said, so that Allah's perfect power would be recognised and His legislation honored.

## "His command descends between them"

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that the verse means divine commands and decrees are revealed and operate throughout the seven heavens and the seven earths, and distinguishes two ways in which they work:

**Tashrīʿī** — legislative. These are the laws divinely prescribed for people who are legally obligated to observe them, revealed through the angels to the Prophets (peace be upon them) to be passed on to humans and jinn. They pertain to articles of faith, worship, good morals, transactions and way of living. Adherence to them attracts reward; flouting them entails punishment.

**Takwīnī** — creative. These are the decrees connected with the creation of the universe, its coming into existence from the realm of non-existence, its gradual growth and development, its depletion and replenishment, and the phenomena of life and death. They encompass the entire divine creation.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out one implication: even if it were proved that between two earths there is atmosphere and distance, and that some kind of creature inhabits it — a creature not legally bound by the Shariʿah laws — the description *"the command descends among them"* would still apply, because Allah's *takwīnī* decrees encompass them as well. And Allah, the Pure and Exalted, knows best.

## What the passage asks of you

- **Read history as evidence, not entertainment.** Ayah 10 calls you a person of understanding precisely at the moment it shows you nations that were destroyed. In Ibn Kathir's words: do not be like them, because if you do, you will suffer what they suffered.
- **Value the two things you have been given.** A Reminder that Allah Himself has undertaken to preserve, and a Messenger ﷺ who recites the Ayat of Allah plain and apparent and explains them. Neither was owed to you.
- **Pair belief with action.** Twice in ayah 11 the promise is tied to faith *and* righteous deeds. That is the door out of the darkness.
- **Let the greatness of Allah change the weight of His commands.** Ibn Kathir says the ayah asserts Allah's perfect power and infinite greatness so that the religion He has legislated is honored and implemented. He has power over all things and surrounds all things with His knowledge — and, as the hadith cited here warns, not even a usurped hand span of land falls outside it.
